findings.body: `datetime.utcnow()` returns a naive datetime, whereas the previous implementation returned a UTC-aware value. Preserve the aware UTC timestamp so callers can safely compare it with other timezone-aware datetimes.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller compares `fetched_at` with an aware datetime; Python raises `TypeError` because one value is naive and the other is aware.
findings.title: Keep the fetched timestamp timezone-aware

findings.title: Replace the deprecated GMT formatter

findings.body: Passing a command string with `shell=True` contradicts the specification's requirement to use an argument vector without a shell. It also lets shell metacharacters in `user_name` alter the command that runs.

findings.body: `user_name` is inserted directly into a string that is executed with `shell=True`, so shell metacharacters in the name can execute arbitrary commands. Pass the executable and arguments as a list to `subprocess.run` instead.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller supplies a user name containing shell syntax; the shell interprets it as a command and executes it while rendering the report.
findings.title: Avoid interpolating the user name into a shell command

findings.title: Return every input row

findings.title: Preserve the default timeout and return shape

findings.body: `std::mem::uninitialized()` creates a `UserRecord` without initializing its fields, which is undefined behavior for ordinary Rust types; passing it to `UserRecord::merge` may already trigger invalid reads or drops. Construct a valid value before merging, or redesign the function so it does not require a fabricated `UserRecord`.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling `fetch_user` creates an invalid `UserRecord` and passes it to `merge`; if its fields are read or dropped, the program has undefined behavior and may crash or behave unpredictably.
findings.title: Remove the uninitialized-value read

findings.anchor: pub fn fetch_user(id: &str, timeout_ms: u64) -> (UserRecord, u64) {
findings.body: The stated intent is to keep `fetch_user` source compatible, but this changes both the parameter from `Option<u64>` to `u64` and the return type from `UserRecord` to `(UserRecord, u64)`. Existing callers using the old signature will no longer compile.
findings.failure_scenario: When an existing caller passes `None` or expects a `UserRecord` return value, compiling against this change fails because the function now requires `u64` and returns a tuple.
findings.title: Preserve the original `fetch_user` signature
